answer:
**RFT means learning from your own attempts after someone checks them.** For each question, sample several solutions, verify their answers, and keep successful examples. Supervised fine-tuning then makes those retained trajectories more likely. If a model generates 20 attempts and three pass a trustworthy check, those three become training examples; the other 17 are usually discarded. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465)

This is particularly useful when the model already sometimes solves the task. It turns an expensive sampling procedure into a cheaper single-attempt policy. STaR is an iterative bootstrapping approach, including mechanisms that use known answers to produce useful rationalizations; it is more specific than merely collecting arbitrary synthetic explanations.

**Why RFT can get stuck.** If no attempt succeeds, filtering produces no training signal for that question. If only one narrow solution style survives, repeated training can reduce exploration. A correct final number also does not guarantee every written reasoning step is valid: accidental success can teach a bad method.

Online RL samples from the changing policy and updates probabilities using rewards or relative advantages. It can use information from failures and optimize graded objectives, but requires managing rollout cost, stability, and exploration. Prefer RFT as a simple baseline when verified successes are plentiful. Consider RL when continued exploration or a richer reward offers measurable benefits. In either case, reserve independent evaluation problems and inspect the verifier before scaling generation.

**Technical details and references.**

Rejection-sampling fine-tuning generates candidate solutions, keeps those passing a correctness check, and trains with supervised likelihood on the retained examples. STaR iterates generation and training, including rationalization mechanisms to bootstrap useful reasoning. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465)

$$\mathcal L_{RFT}=-\sum_{(x,y):verify(y)=1}\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x).$$

RFT is simple when enough correct diverse samples exist and verification is strong. It discards unsuccessful trajectories and can narrow diversity or reinforce flawed rationales that happen to reach correct answers. Online RL explicitly uses relative reward and exploration from the current policy, but has more optimization and rollout complexity. Start with verified supervised data when feasible; use RL when the objective benefits from ongoing exploration and the reward signal withstands exploitation.
